q: The paper handles G/N cyclic via Theorem 10 to build a coset-rep set V of size O(log|G/N|); for non-cyclic G/N it defaults to enumerating all |G/N| coset reps. Is there an intermediate regime (metacyclic, nilpotent-of-small-class, or class-2 factor groups) in which a poly(log|G/N|)-size V still exists but the Theorem 13 template cannot exploit it, forcing exponential blowup that could be avoided by a different reduction?
basis: During the k=2..6 reproduction only G/N = Z_2 (single non-trivial coset rep, |V|=1) was exercised. The paper's paragraph directly after Theorem 13's proof drops the cyclic assumption without giving a poly-time algorithm — the practical cutoff is unclear from the text and the reproduction did not stress-test it.
next_steps: Extend the code to G = (Z_2)^k semidirect Z_2^m for m=2,3 with a fixed action and measure how (a) |V| grows and (b) whether the |V|-many Abelian-HSP subproblems each still concentrate on their K^perp with probability 1. If they do, try to push m up to 4-5 and see when classical post-processing time dominates.

q: For hidden subgroups H of order > 2 (i.e. H = <(u1,1)> extended by a nontrivial H_0 = H \cap N), does the empirical sample-complexity curve (medians per k) actually improve as |H| grows, because |K| grows and |K^perp| shrinks? The paper's O(log|G|) bound is worst-case in H — is the average-case bound tighter?
basis: All 15 tested instances used |H|=2 (a single reflection). Median samples for full recovery came out at (k+1) very consistently — but this is the maximum-|K^perp| = minimum-|K| edge case. A generic |H|=4 or |H|=8 case would give shorter K^perp lists and might collapse to O(1) additional samples.
next_steps: Add a sweep parameterised by dim(H \cap N) in {0,1,2,3} on top of k=4,5,6 and plot median samples-to-recover vs. |H|. Compare against the coupon-collector bound (k+1) - log2(|H|) and the theorem's O(log|G|).

q: The reduction demands two invocations of f per index — f((x,0)) for the b=0 branch and f((x,1)) for the b=1 branch. In a coherent-oracle model, is there a controlled-z construction that folds F into a single query, halving the oracle-query complexity? Or is the factor-of-two overhead inherent to reducing a non-Abelian coset problem to an Abelian one?
basis: The reproduction implemented F literally as two disjoint table lookups (see build_F_table in ims_theorem13.py). No attempt was made at a coherent single-query implementation. The paper does not discuss query-complexity constants.
next_steps: Try a Qiskit implementation where the b register controls a coherent SWAP of the group-element register with the z-shifted version before a single call to the coherent U_f, and count exact oracle queries. Compare with the naive two-call variant on a shot-noise circuit simulator to verify equal output distributions.

q: The Theorem 13 reduction crucially exploits that Z_2 x N is Abelian because N is elementary abelian 2. Our negative-control (dihedral_hsp.py) shows the same F-construction FAILS for D_n with N = Z_n and n odd — the derived K is not even a subgroup. What is the smallest non-elementary-abelian N (e.g. N = Z_4, N = Z_2 x Z_4, N = Z_9) for which a modified reduction with a different linearisation still yields an Abelian-HSP-solvable auxiliary function?
basis: The dihedral_hsp.py control confirmed that only N = Z_4 with d = 2 and N = Z_6 with d = 3 (i.e. 2d ≡ 0 mod n) gave the theorem's clean 100 percent-on-lattice behaviour — every other case gave partial mass. This suggests the reduction is very sensitive to the 2-torsion structure of N.
next_steps: Try N = Z_2 x Z_4 or Z_2 x Z_2 x Z_4 with H = <(u,1)> where u has order 2, and check whether the resulting F on Z_2 x N still hides a subgroup of Z_2 x N. If yes, this would enlarge the class covered by Theorem 13 with only a mild modification.

q: Our post-processing step recovers K from K^perp samples by classical Gaussian elimination over F_2 in O((k+1)^3) time. The paper is silent on whether a coherent alternative — e.g. amplitude-amplifying K^perp sampling combined with a HHL-style quantum linear-algebra step for the final kernel computation — could give any asymptotic speedup, or whether the abelian-HSP subroutine is already tight against a matching quantum lower bound.
basis: The empirical (k+1) samples matches the coupon-collector upper bound within a small constant. No published matching quantum lower bound exists for the |H|-recovery cost inside a semidirect-product HSP; a tightness question is natural but not addressed by the paper.
next_steps: Do a literature scan post-2001 (Kuperberg 2003, Regev 2004, Bacon-Childs-van Dam 2005) for any lower-bound work that specialises to G = N semidirect Z_2 with N elementary abelian 2, and if none exists, run a Grover-amplified simulation to see whether O(sqrt(k)) samples suffice or whether O(k) is genuinely the sample-optimal rate for pure-state Fourier sampling.
